item.title: Small Talk
item.description:
It was a sticky day outside the church. The air wrapped around and between the leaves while the boys sat together and watched cars grind north on Third Avenue.

Steve tapped his black shoes together. “I’m hungry.”

“Yeah, it was a lousy lunch. Those sandwiches were like the ones from school.”

Steve nodded. “So bad, soggy too.”

“I’ll make you something tonight, maybe tortellini.”

Steve smiled and closed his eyes. “So where’s Mom now?”

item.title: Last Table
item.description:
The restaurant was closing for good on Sunday. Roberto had owned it for thirty-one years and his knees had owned it for about twenty-five.

“How many covers tonight?” asked his daughter, who did the books and worried about the things Roberto refused to worry about.

“Forty-two. We could do sixty if we pushed the tables together.”

“We’re not pushing the tables together.”

“I know.”

The last seating was at nine. Roberto had considered making it earlier but nine felt right. People should eat late on the last night. They should linger. They should order dessert even if they never order dessert.

item.title: Night Swim
item.description:
The pool was heated but the air was not, and the distance between the two was the whole problem. Claire stood at the edge in her suit and counted.

“Just jump,” said Marco from the water. His voice echoed off the concrete walls of the hotel courtyard. It was after midnight and they were not supposed to be here.

“I’m going to jump.”

“You’ve been saying that.”

“I’m building up to it.”

item.title: The Mountain
item.description:
They had been climbing for four hours when Paul stopped and said he couldn’t feel his hands.

“Wiggle your fingers,” said Ray, who was ahead by ten feet and did not turn around.

“I’m wiggling them.”

“Can you feel them wiggling?”

Paul looked at his gloves. His fingers were moving inside them but the sensation was remote, like watching someone else’s hands. “Sort of.”

Ray finally turned. His face was red from the wind and his goggles were pushed up on his forehead. He looked like a man who had just been told something he already knew.

item.title: Tuesday Morning
item.description:
The coffee shop on Seventh had exactly one good table. It was near the window but not against it, close enough to watch the street but far enough that you didn’t feel watched. Daniel always sat there.

“You’re here early,” said the barista, whose name was either Amy or Annie. Daniel had never asked and it was now too late to ask.

“Couldn’t sleep.”

“Bad dreams?”

“No dreams at all. That’s worse, I think.”

item.title: The Lamp
item.description:
The lamp had been in the window for as long as anyone on the block could remember. It was brass, or something like brass, with a shade the color of old paper.

Margaret turned it on every evening at six and turned it off when she went to bed. She had done this since her husband died, which was eleven years ago, or maybe twelve. She could not remember the exact year anymore, only the season. It was fall.
